paragraphs: The rest of the argument against the Constitution's provisions on taxation is built on the following clause. The last clause of the eighth section of the first article of the plan under consideration authorizes the national legislature "to make all laws which shall be NECESSARY and PROPER for carrying into execution THE POWERS by that Constitution vested in the government of the United States, or in any department or officer thereof." And the second clause of the sixth article declares "that the Constitution and the laws of the United States made IN PURSUANCE THEREOF, and the treaties made by their authority shall be the SUPREME LAW of the land, any thing in the constitution or laws of any State to the contrary notwithstanding."

These two clauses have drawn a flood of bitter invective and petulant declamation against the proposed Constitution. They have been held up to the people, in every exaggerated color of misrepresentation, as destructive engines meant to destroy their local governments and wipe out their liberties. They have been called a hideous monster whose devouring jaws would spare neither sex nor age, neither high nor low, neither sacred nor profane. Yet, strange as it may seem after all this clamor, anyone who has not happened to view them in the same light may be assured with perfect confidence that the intended government would operate, constitutionally, in exactly the same way if these clauses were struck out entirely as if they were repeated in every article. They merely declare a truth that would follow by necessary and unavoidable implication from the very act of constituting a federal government and giving it certain specified powers. The proposition is so clear that even moderation itself can hardly listen to the railings so copiously poured out against this part of the plan without feeling its calm disturbed.

What is a power, if not the ability or faculty of doing a thing? What is the ability to do a thing, if not the power of using the MEANS necessary to carry it out? What is a LEGISLATIVE power, if not a power of making LAWS? What are the MEANS of carrying out a LEGISLATIVE power, if not LAWS? What is the power of laying and collecting taxes, if not a LEGISLATIVE POWER, a power of MAKING LAWS to lay and collect taxes? And what are the proper means of carrying out such a power, if not NECESSARY and PROPER laws?

This simple line of inquiry gives us at once a test for judging the true nature of the clause complained of. It brings us to this plain truth: a power to lay and collect taxes must be a power to pass all laws NECESSARY and PROPER for carrying out that power. And what does the unfortunate and slandered provision do beyond declaring the same truth, namely that the national legislature, to which the power of laying and collecting taxes had already been given, might in carrying out that power pass all laws NECESSARY and PROPER to give it effect? I have applied these observations in particular to the power of taxation because it is the subject now before us, and because it is the most important of the authorities proposed to be conferred on the Union. But the same process will lead to the same result for all the other powers declared in the Constitution. It is EXPRESSLY to carry out these powers that the sweeping clause, as it has been affectedly called, authorizes the national legislature to pass all NECESSARY and PROPER laws. If anything is objectionable, the objection must be looked for in the specific powers on which this general declaration rests. The declaration itself may be charged with tautology or redundancy, but it is perfectly harmless.

But SUSPICION may ask why it was introduced, then. The answer is that it could only have been done out of extra caution, to guard against every quibbling refinement by those who might later feel inclined to curtail and evade the legitimate authorities of the Union. The Convention probably foresaw what these papers have chiefly aimed to impress: that the danger most threatening to our political welfare is that the State governments will in the end undermine the foundations of the Union. On so cardinal a point it may therefore have thought it necessary to leave nothing to construction. Whatever moved it to include the clause, the wisdom of the precaution is plain from the outcry raised against it, since that very outcry betrays a readiness to question the great and essential truth which the provision was manifestly meant to declare.

But it may be asked again: who is to judge of the NECESSITY and PROPRIETY of the laws to be passed for carrying out the powers of the Union? My first answer is that this question arises just as fully on the simple grant of those powers as on the declaratory clause. My second is that the national government, like every other, must judge in the first instance of the proper exercise of its powers, and its constituents in the last. Suppose the federal government should overstep the just bounds of its authority and use its powers tyrannically. The people, whose creature it is, must then appeal to the standard they have set up, and take whatever measures to redress the injury done to the Constitution the emergency may suggest and prudence justify. The propriety of a law, in a constitutional light, must always be decided by the nature of the powers on which it is founded. Suppose that, by some forced construction of its authority (which indeed can hardly be imagined), the federal legislature should try to change the law of descent in some State. Would it not be evident that in making such an attempt it had exceeded its jurisdiction and infringed on that of the State? Suppose again that, on the pretense of interference with its revenues, it should undertake to abolish a land tax imposed by the authority of a State. Would it not be equally evident that this was an invasion of the concurrent jurisdiction in this kind of tax which the Constitution plainly supposes the State governments to have? If any doubt on this point should ever arise, the blame will lie entirely with those reasoners who, in the imprudent zeal of their hostility to the plan of the Convention, have labored to wrap it in a cloud meant to hide the plainest and simplest truths.

But it is said that the laws of the Union are to be the SUPREME LAW of the land. What can be inferred from this? And what would those laws amount to if they were not supreme? Plainly, nothing. A LAW, by the very meaning of the term, includes supremacy. It is a rule that those to whom it is given are bound to obey. This follows from every political association. When individuals enter into a state of society, the laws of that society must be the supreme regulator of their conduct. When a number of political societies enter into a larger political society, the laws that the larger one enacts in accordance with the powers entrusted to it by its constitution must necessarily be supreme over those societies and over the individuals who compose them. Otherwise it would be a mere treaty, dependent on the good faith of the parties, and not a government, which is only another word for POLITICAL POWER AND SUPREMACY. But it does not follow from this doctrine that acts of the larger society which are NOT PURSUANT to its constitutional powers, and which invade the residuary authorities of the smaller societies, will become the supreme law of the land. Such acts will be mere usurpation and will deserve to be treated as such. So we see that the clause declaring the supremacy of the laws of the Union, like the one we have just examined, only declares a truth that flows immediately and necessarily from the institution of a federal government. It will not, I presume, have escaped notice that the clause EXPRESSLY confines this supremacy to laws made PURSUANT TO THE CONSTITUTION. I mention this merely as an instance of the Convention's caution, since the limitation would have been understood even if it had not been stated.

Therefore, a law laying a tax for the use of the United States would be supreme in its nature and could not legally be opposed or controlled. But a law abolishing or preventing the collection of a tax laid by the authority of a State (unless on imports and exports) would not be the supreme law of the land; it would be a usurpation of power not granted by the Constitution. An improper pile-up of taxes on the same object might make collection difficult or uncertain. That would be a problem for both sides, arising not from superior or defective power on either side but from an unwise use of power by one or the other, in a manner equally disadvantageous to both. It is to be hoped and presumed, however, that mutual interest would dictate coordination in this respect and so avoid any serious problem. The inference from the whole is that under the proposed Constitution the individual States would keep an independent and uncontrollable authority to raise revenue, to whatever extent they may need, by every kind of taxation except duties on imports and exports. It will be shown in the next paper that this CONCURRENT JURISDICTION in taxation was the only admissible substitute for the complete subordination of State authority to that of the Union in this branch of power.
